questions.q: Which of the following best describes a single entry bookkeeping system?
options: A complete accounting system where every transaction has an equal debit and credit entry
A system where typically only cash transactions and personal accounts of debtors and creditors are maintained
A system that uses only nominal accounts to calculate daily profits
A system recognized by International Financial Reporting Standards as the most perfect for large corporations
questions.explain: A **single entry system** is an incomplete form of bookkeeping where the strict rule of double entry is not followed. Usually, only the Cash Book and personal accounts of customers (debtors) and suppliers (creditors) are kept, while real and nominal accounts (like assets and expenses) are largely ignored.

questions.q: All the following are distinct limitations of keeping accounting records under the single entry system EXCEPT that
options: It is difficult to prepare a trial balance to check the arithmetical accuracy of the books
The preparation of reliable final accounts is impossible without lengthy conversions
It provides a highly detailed and exhaustive breakdown of all nominal accounts and indirect expenses
It is generally deemed inadequate for tax assessment purposes by tax authorities
questions.explain: Because a single entry system ignores most double-entry principles, it **does not** keep a detailed track of nominal accounts (incomes and expenses). Thus, stating that it provides a detailed breakdown of nominal accounts (Option C) is false and is not a limitation—it's an inaccurate characteristic.
